screens.title: What is Foundry?
screens.narratorSegment: Foundry is a toolchain for Ethereum development written in Rust and designed around minimal context switching for Solidity developers. Its three pillars are Forge for compiling, testing and running scripts, Cast for command-line interactions with the EVM, and Anvil as a local node for testing. The Solidity-first approach means you can write tests and deployment logic directly in Solidity instead of JavaScript. That matters because it reduces translation errors between test and contract code and can improve speed for large test suites. A concrete example is writing a deployer contract that calls vm. startBroadcast, creates a new contract instance, and then stops broadcasting; everything is compiled and executed by Forge. A common misconception is that Rust under the hood changes Solidity behaviour. It does not: Foundry compiles and executes Solidity like other toolchains, but its Rust implementation focuses on performance and CLI ergonomics. Key takeaway: Foundry keeps you inside the language you write contracts in while giving you fast, CLI-first tools for development. What is Foundry? means foundry bundles forge, cast, and anvil to let you write, deploy, and interact with contracts while staying in solidity.. In practical terms, a solidity-first toolkit with forge, cast, and anvil. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Install and Initialize a Foundry Project
screens.narratorSegment: Getting started with Foundry begins with its installer and a project scaffold. Use foundryup to install the toolchain; it's the recommended installer that fetches Forge, Cast, and Anvil. After installation, run forge init my-foundry-project to create a new project. The init command scaffolds a workspace with src, lib, script, and test directories. Source files belong in src; third-party dependencies appear under lib; deployment scripts go into script; and behavioral tests go in test. This structure keeps concerns separated and makes deployments repeatable. A concrete use case: you want a reproducible environment for CI — the forge init layout supports adding a dependency via forge install and committing lib/ as a submodule. Common mistake: initializing inside another project or forgetting to configure your shell to load foundryup paths. Key takeaway: initialize early, inspect the directories, and commit minimal configuration so your team shares the same structure. screens.title: Project Structure Explained
screens.narratorSegment: A predictable layout makes it faster to find contracts and scripts. In a Foundry project, src/ contains your smart contracts, written in Solidity. Use lib/ to manage dependencies such as OpenZeppelin contracts; you can add them with forge install which places them under lib as submodules. The script/ folder is reserved for Forge scripts—Solidity contracts that inherit from Script. sol and implement a run function to execute deployment logic. The test/ folder holds Solidity tests that Forge executes. A concrete example: your Greeter contract lives in src/Greeter. sol, a deploy script in script/DeployGreeter. s. sol, and tests in test/Greeter. t. sol. This separation helps CI and local workflows: CI runs forge test, and deploy pipelines run forge script. A common misconception is that script/ should contain JavaScript; in Foundry it should contain Solidity scripts. Key takeaway: follow the convention and you reduce cognitive overhead when collaborating. screens.title: Forge Scripts in Solidity
screens.narratorSegment: Forge scripts are Solidity contracts that inherit from Script. sol and implement a run function that Forge executes. Within run, you can call vm helper functions provided by Foundry to manipulate execution and sign transactions. For deployment you normally start broadcasting with vm. startBroadcast or vm. broadcast, deploy contracts using new ContractName(args), and then call vm. stopBroadcast to stop sending signed transactions. An example flow: call vm. startBroadcast with the private key supplied via environment variable or CLI flag, deploy your contract, then stop broadcasting and log the deployed address. A common misconception is that vm. startBroadcast is optional; in simulations it is, but to actually send signed transactions you must use either vm. startBroadcast or the --broadcast flag with forge script. Practical tip: do not hardcode private keys in scripts; rely on environment variables or a keystore. The key takeaway is that Forge scripts give you on-chain control while remaining in Solidity, but they require explicit broadcasting to move from simulation to real transactions. content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Forge Scripts
Script Anatomy
import 'forge-std/Script.sol';

contract DeployExample is Script {
  function run() public {
    vm.startBroadcast();
    Example e = new Example();
    vm.stopBroadcast();
  }
}
vm.startBroadcast reads the private key from environment or CLI and signs subsequent transactions until vm.stopBroadcast. This is how simulations become real deployments.
Usage Tips
  • Use run() to encapsulate deploy steps so forge executes them deterministically.
  • Log addresses with console.log for verification after deployment.
  • Avoid embedding secrets; use environment variables or keystore files.
Misconception
Forgetting that tests and scripts can both be written in Solidity; tests are executed with forge test, scripts with forge script.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Greeter Example
src/Greeter.sol
// src/Greeter.sol
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.20;

contract Greeter {
  string private _greeting;

  constructor(string memory greeting_) {
    _greeting = greeting_;
  }

  function greet() public view returns (string memory) {
    return _greeting;
  }

  function setGreeting(string memory greeting_) public {
    _greeting = greeting_;
  }
}
script/DeployGreeter.s.sol
// script/DeployGreeter.s.sol
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.20;

import 'forge-std/Script.sol';
import '../src/Greeter.sol';

contract DeployGreeter is Script {
  function run() public returns (Greeter greeter) {
    vm.startBroadcast();
    greeter = new Greeter('Hello, Foundry!');
    vm.stopBroadcast();
    console.log('Greeter deployed to:', address(greeter));
  }
}
Notice how the deployment is literal: new Greeter constructs the contract and the script controls broadcasting. Keep secrets out of the source.

screens.title: Running forge script — flags explained
screens.narratorSegment: Executing a deployment script uses the forge script command with a few important flags that change runtime behavior. The command identifies the script file and contract to run, but it will only simulate by default. The --rpc-url flag points Forge to the network RPC, enabling it to connect to Sepolia or another network. The --broadcast flag instructs Forge to stop simulating and to actually sign and send transactions using the private key from FOUNDRY_PRIVATE_KEY or the CLI. The --verify flag attempts explorer verification after deployment, which requires an ETHERSCAN_API_KEY. Additional verbosity flags, like -vvvv, increase logging and help debug gas and transaction details. A common pitfall is forgetting --broadcast; you may see a successful simulation but no on-chain deployment. Practical example: set FOUNDRY_PRIVATE_KEY and SEPOLIA_RPC_URL in your environment, then run forge script script/DeployGreeter. s. sol:DeployGreeter --rpc-url $SEPOLIA_RPC_URL --broadcast --verify -vvvv to deploy and verify. Key takeaway: treat --broadcast as the deliberate step that turns simulation into an on-chain event. Running forge script — flags explained means --rpc-url connects to a network; --broadcast sends real transactions; --verify requests explorer verification; verbosity aids debugging.. In practical terms, how rpc, broadcast, verify, and verbosity change behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Using Cast to Interact with Deployed Contracts
screens.narratorSegment: Cast is Foundry’s command-line utility for interacting with the EVM. Use cast call to execute view or pure functions without signing transactions; it returns the function result. Use cast send for state-changing actions; cast send signs and broadcasts a transaction when given a private key. For example, to read a Greeter's greeting you would run cast call "greet()(string)" --rpc-url your_rpc. The function signature lists the inputs and the return types, where the return type is in parentheses. To set a new greeting you would run cast send "setGreeting(string)" "New greeting" --private-key $FOUNDRY_PRIVATE_KEY --rpc-url your_rpc. A common confusion is mixing view and send: cast call is free and requires no key, whereas cast send consumes gas and requires signing. Practical tip: keep the command signatures handy and verify the expected return type in the call string. Key takeaway: Cast provides fast CLI access to read state and send transactions after deployment. In practical terms, cast call for reads, cast send for signed transactions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Deploy MyNFT
src/MyNFT.sol (excerpt)
// src/MyNFT.sol
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.20;

import '@openzeppelin/contracts/token/ERC721/ERC721.sol';
import '@openzeppelin/contracts/access/Ownable.sol';
import '@openzeppelin/contracts/utils/Counters.sol';

contract MyNFT is ERC721, Ownable {
  using Counters for Counters.Counter;
  Counters.Counter private _tokenIdCounter;

  constructor() ERC721('Cohortia NFT', 'CNFT') Ownable(msg.sender) {}

  function safeMint(address to) public onlyOwner {
    uint256 tokenId = _tokenIdCounter.current();
    _tokenIdCounter.increment();
    _safeMint(to, tokenId);
  }
}
Deployment script
forge install OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts --no-commit
forge script script/DeployMyNFT.s.sol:DeployMyNFT --rpc-url $SEPOLIA_RPC_URL --broadcast --verify -vvvv
After deployment, mint an NFT via cast send and then confirm the owner with cast call balanceOf.
Key Takeaway
This sequence demonstrates a full deploy-test-verify cycle for an ERC-721 using Solidity-first scripts and CLI tooling.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Security Notes
screens.narratorSegment: When deploying with Foundry, several practical pitfalls can interrupt your flow. The most common is forgetting the --broadcast flag: without it, forge script runs only a simulation and no on-chain transaction is emitted. Another frequent issue is misconfigured FOUNDRY_PRIVATE_KEY or RPC URLs; always verify environment variables are set and the deployer account is funded. Gas problems can still occur: specify gas-price or priority-gas-price if network conditions demand it. Security-wise, never hardcode private keys in scripts or commit. env files to source control; prefer environment variables or a keystore file that Foundry supports. Foundry also supports keystore management which is a safer production practice. Finally, remember Solidity scripting can feel verbose for complex off-chain logic — sometimes a JavaScript pipeline is still appropriate for orchestration. Key takeaway: adopt safe key handling, confirm broadcast intent, and validate gas before deploying live to avoid costly mistakes. screens.title: Foundry vs Hardhat

fullNarratorScript:
Foundry is a fast, Rust-based toolkit that lets you remain in Solidity while you compile, test, script, and deploy. In this lesson you will learn how Foundry’s three components—Forge, Cast, and Anvil—fit together, how to initialize a project, and how to write a Forge script that deploys a contract from Solidity. We will step through a minimal Greeter example and a hands-on ERC-721 NFT deployment to Sepolia, and we will cover the common pitfalls you must avoid, such as forgetting to broadcast transactions and protecting private keys. You will also see how Cast lets you query contract state and send transactions from the command line. By the end, you’ll understand why some teams prefer a Solidity-first workflow and how this affects scripting style, debugging, and security. Think about the last time you switched languages to script deployments; Foundry aims to remove that friction. As you move through the screens, watch the example commands and scripts and consider how vm functions like startBroadcast change the deployment lifecycle.

Over the next screens you will set up a Foundry project, write deployment scripts in Solidity using Forge, and interact with deployed contracts using Cast. First, you will initialize a new project and inspect the folder layout so you know where contracts, scripts, and tests live. Next, you will write a Forge script that inherits from Script. sol, use vm functions to broadcast transactions, and perform an actual deployment to Sepolia. You will also practice using Cast to call view functions and send signed transactions from the command line. Finally, you'll compare Foundry and Hardhat, learn common mistakes to avoid, and complete a hands-on NFT deployment. Each objective pairs a practical skill with a practical reason: keeping scripts in Solidity reduces context switching, Cast provides quick CLI checks, and Anvil speeds local iteration. By the end you'll be able to demonstrate a deployment pipeline and explain the trade-offs when choosing a tooling stack.

These objectives emphasize practical actions you will perform. First, you will run the forge init command to scaffold a project and inspect the directories it creates. Then you will author a deployment script in Solidity that calls vm. startBroadcast and vm. stopBroadcast so transactions are sent. You will deploy a Greeter contract and an ERC-721 NFT to Sepolia and verify the deployment flow using forge script with the broadcast and verify flags. Finally, you will use cast call to read state and cast send to invoke state-changing methods. Each action has a clear success signal: a deployed contract address, a successful cast call output, or a verified contract on the explorer. Practice these steps in order to avoid common mistakes such as simulating without broadcasting or leaking private keys. This hands-on sequence is the fastest way to internalize Foundry’s scripting model.

Foundry is a toolchain for Ethereum development written in Rust and designed around minimal context switching for Solidity developers. Its three pillars are Forge for compiling, testing and running scripts, Cast for command-line interactions with the EVM, and Anvil as a local node for testing. The Solidity-first approach means you can write tests and deployment logic directly in Solidity instead of JavaScript. That matters because it reduces translation errors between test and contract code and can improve speed for large test suites. A concrete example is writing a deployer contract that calls vm. startBroadcast, creates a new contract instance, and then stops broadcasting; everything is compiled and executed by Forge. A common misconception is that Rust under the hood changes Solidity behaviour. It does not: Foundry compiles and executes Solidity like other toolchains, but its Rust implementation focuses on performance and CLI ergonomics. Key takeaway: Foundry keeps you inside the language you write contracts in while giving you fast, CLI-first tools for development. What is Foundry? means foundry bundles forge, cast, and anvil to let you write, deploy, and interact with contracts while staying in solidity.. In practical terms, a solidity-first toolkit with forge, cast, and anvil. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Getting started with Foundry begins with its installer and a project scaffold. Use foundryup to install the toolchain; it's the recommended installer that fetches Forge, Cast, and Anvil. After installation, run forge init my-foundry-project to create a new project. The init command scaffolds a workspace with src, lib, script, and test directories. Forge scripts are Solidity contracts that inherit from Script. sol and implement a run function that Forge executes. Within run, you can call vm helper functions provided by Foundry to manipulate execution and sign transactions. For deployment you normally start broadcasting with vm. startBroadcast or vm. broadcast, deploy contracts using new ContractName(args), and then call vm. stopBroadcast to stop sending signed transactions. An example flow: call vm. startBroadcast with the private key supplied via environment variable or CLI flag, deploy your contract, then stop broadcasting and log the deployed address. A common misconception is that vm. startBroadcast is optional; in simulations it is, but to actually send signed transactions you must use either vm. startBroadcast or the --broadcast flag with forge script. Practical tip: do not hardcode private keys in scripts; rely on environment variables or a keystore. The key takeaway is that Forge scripts give you on-chain control while remaining in Solidity, but they require explicit broadcasting to move from simulation to real transactions. Executing a deployment script uses the forge script command with a few important flags that change runtime behavior. The command identifies the script file and contract to run, but it will only simulate by default. The --rpc-url flag points Forge to the network RPC, enabling it to connect to Sepolia or another network. The --broadcast flag instructs Forge to stop simulating and to actually sign and send transactions using the private key from FOUNDRY_PRIVATE_KEY or the CLI. The --verify flag attempts explorer verification after deployment, which requires an ETHERSCAN_API_KEY. Additional verbosity flags, like -vvvv, increase logging and help debug gas and transaction details. A common pitfall is forgetting --broadcast; you may see a successful simulation but no on-chain deployment. Practical example: set FOUNDRY_PRIVATE_KEY and SEPOLIA_RPC_URL in your environment, then run forge script script/DeployGreeter. s. sol:DeployGreeter --rpc-url $SEPOLIA_RPC_URL --broadcast --verify -vvvv to deploy and verify. Key takeaway: treat --broadcast as the deliberate step that turns simulation into an on-chain event. Cast is Foundry’s command-line utility for interacting with the EVM. Use cast call to execute view or pure functions without signing transactions; it returns the function result. Use cast send for state-changing actions; cast send signs and broadcasts a transaction when given a private key. For example, to read a Greeter's greeting you would run cast call "greet()(string)" --rpc-url your_rpc. The function signature lists the inputs and the return types, where the return type is in parentheses. To set a new greeting you would run cast send "setGreeting(string)" "New greeting" --private-key $FOUNDRY_PRIVATE_KEY --rpc-url your_rpc. A common confusion is mixing view and send: cast call is free and requires no key, whereas cast send consumes gas and requires signing. Practical tip: keep the command signatures handy and verify the expected return type in the call string. Key takeaway: Cast provides fast CLI access to read state and send transactions after deployment. Because Anvil starts quickly and pairs well with forge and cast, you can run full deploy-and-test cycles locally without network latency. When deploying with Foundry, several practical pitfalls can interrupt your flow. The most common is forgetting the --broadcast flag: without it, forge script runs only a simulation and no on-chain transaction is emitted. Another frequent issue is misconfigured FOUNDRY_PRIVATE_KEY or RPC URLs; always verify environment variables are set and the deployer account is funded. Gas problems can still occur: specify gas-price or priority-gas-price if network conditions demand it. Security-wise, never hardcode private keys in scripts or commit. env files to source control; prefer environment variables or a keystore file that Foundry supports. Foundry also supports keystore management which is a safer production practice. Finally, remember Solidity scripting can feel verbose for complex off-chain logic — sometimes a JavaScript pipeline is still appropriate for orchestration. Key takeaway: adopt safe key handling, confirm broadcast intent, and validate gas before deploying live to avoid costly mistakes. Local nodes differ: Hardhat Network is the built-in dev node for Hardhat, while Anvil is Foundry’s high-performance local EVM. For CLI interactions, Hardhat scripts commonly use ethers. js, whereas Foundry uses Cast for quick command-line calls. Hardhat often feels familiar to JavaScript teams; Foundry appeals to those who prefer staying inside Solidity.
